clinicalPearls: A group of related disorders in which follicular keratosis is accompanied by inflammation that heals with atrophic scarring, distinguishing it from ordinary keratosis pilaris
Ulerythema ophryogenes affects the eyebrows and lateral cheeks with follicular papules, erythema and later loss of the outer eyebrows
Atrophoderma vermiculatum causes a distinctive worm-eaten (honeycomb) pitted scarring of the cheeks, usually beginning in childhood
Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans is the most severe variant, with widespread spiny follicular keratosis and scarring alopecia
Some cases occur in isolation while others are associated with syndromes such as Noonan and cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes or with MBTPS2-related disease
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by biopsy showing follicular hyperkeratosis, perifollicular inflammation and dermal fibrosis; genetic testing is guided by the phenotype
Management is supportive with emollients and keratolytics, anti-inflammatory measures for the erythema, and cosmetic treatment such as laser for residual redness once inflammation settles
reference.pathophysiology: Keratosis pilaris atrophicans encompasses several disorders sharing abnormal follicular keratinisation with a significant inflammatory component. Keratotic plugging of follicles is accompanied by perifollicular inflammation that, unlike simple keratosis pilaris, damages the follicle and surrounding dermis and heals with atrophy and scarring, hence the eyebrow loss, honeycomb facial atrophy or scarring alopecia depending on the variant. Genetic contributions vary, ranging from isolated dominant traits to association with RASopathies such as Noonan and cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes and with MBTPS2-related keratinisation disorders at the severe end of the spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans and IFAP syndrome
Discoid lupus erythematosus (for scarring facial lesions)
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing follicular hyperkeratosis, perifollicular inflammation and dermal fibrosis
Assessment for associated syndromes (Noonan, cardiofaciocutaneous) including cardiac and developmental review
Molecular genetic testing guided by phenotype (e.g. RASopathy genes, MBTPS2)
Trichoscopy and dermoscopy of affected areas
Clinical photography to monitor scarring and erythema
redFlags: Progressive scarring alopecia suggesting the severe decalvans variant
Dysmorphic, cardiac or developmental features indicating an associated RASopathy
Secondary infection of inflamed follicular lesions
reference.prognosis: The inflammatory phase and follicular keratosis often improve after puberty, but any atrophic scarring, eyebrow loss or scarring alopecia is permanent; overall prognosis depends on whether an underlying syndrome is present.
pitfalls: Dismissing early disease as ordinary keratosis pilaris and missing the scarring potential
Overlooking an associated RASopathy such as Noonan or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome
Using ablative cosmetic treatments while active inflammation persists
Failing to recognise the continuum with keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans and IFAP syndrome
